basis: Cell counts and biomass set how many cells react; per-cell rates come from maintenance power and signalling studies. Counts all enzyme turnovers (including passive reversible catalysis near k_B T ln 2 = 2.9×10⁻²¹ J); strictly irreversible ATP-hydrolysing steps in the 14 TW prokaryotic budget are bounded by ≤1.7×10³² ATP/s (at ΔG_ATP ≈ 8.3×10⁻²⁰ J, Milo & Phillips 2015).
equation: C_chem = N_prok × c_cell + N_euk × 2,000 a second, where c_cell = 10 (deep rock) × f_deep + 150 (starved) × f_starved + 5,000 (surface) × f_surface
cite: Milo, R., & Phillips, R. (2015). Cell Biology by the Numbers. Garland Science.

basis: Prokaryote abundance in soil, ocean, seafloor and deep continental crust, with carbon per cell.
equation: N_cells = B_prok ÷ 25 fg carbon per cell

basis: Counts of the animals that hold most neurons (nematodes, arthropods, vertebrates) and neurons and synapses per animal. Uses 0.1 signals per synapse per second as the global biosphere mean (dominated by resting cold-blooded nematodes and arthropods), whereas waking active mammal/primate benchmarks in the Atlas use ~1 Hz per synapse (~1.5×10¹⁴ signals/s for a human brain).
equation: C_nerve = synapses × 0.1 signals per synapse per second
cite: Attwell, D., & Laughlin, S. B. (2001). An energy budget for signaling in the grey matter of the brain. J. Cereb. Blood Flow Metab., 21(10), 1133–1145. | Herculano-Houzel, S. (2009). The human brain in numbers. Front. Hum. Neurosci., 3, 31.

basis: Counts of nematodes, arthropods and vertebrates times neurons per individual. A count by animal group (21 Nov 2026) gives about 6×10²³ today: roundworms 1.3×10²³, land arthropods about 5×10²³, fish 10²², people 7×10²⁰. The census's 3.4×10²⁴ is about five times higher, mostly because it assumes 200,000 neurons per land arthropod, where mites and springtails, most of them, hold far fewer. Sea arthropods such as copepods are not yet counted.
equation: N_neurons = synapses ÷ 875 synapses per neuron; today checked against animal counts × neurons per animal
cite: van den Hoogen, J., et al. (2019). Soil nematode abundance and functional group composition at a global scale. Nature, 572, 194–198. | Rosenberg, Y., et al. (2023). The global biomass and number of terrestrial arthropods. Science Advances, 9(5), eabq4049. | Bar-On, Y. M., Phillips, R., & Milo, R. (2018). The biomass distribution on Earth. PNAS, 115(25), 6506–6511.

basis: Installed computing capacity and utilisation: Phister (1979) mainframe census for 1965 (2×10⁹ ops/s), Hilbert & López (2011) global general-purpose and DSP/GPU inventories for 2000–2012 (~19% mean duty cycle: 4.5×10¹⁷ in 2000, 1.8×10²⁰ in 2010, 3.5×10²⁰ in 2012), and Epoch AI / datacenter inventories for 2020–2026 (1.89×10²² executed ops/s today).
equation: C_silicon = installed hardware capacity × mean duty-cycle utilisation (Phister 1979; Hilbert & López 2011; Epoch AI 2025)
cite: Hilbert, M., & López, P. (2011). The world's technological capacity to store, communicate, and compute information. Science, 332(6025), 60–65. | Phister, M. (1979). Data Processing Technology and Economics (2nd ed.). Digital Press.

basis: Accelerator inventory and utilisation for neural-network workloads.
equation: C_AI = 1.5×10⁷ AI chips (H100-class) × 10¹⁵ operations a second × 60% busy

basis: Neuron counts of the largest brains through time up to 2000 CE (~1.5×10¹⁴ signals/s for Homo sapiens); TOP500 #1 Linpack Rmax supercomputers for 2010 (Tianhe-1A, 2.57×10¹⁵), 2012 (Titan, 1.76×10¹⁶) and 2020 (Fugaku, 4.42×10¹⁷); and one 100,000-GPU frontier AI cluster in 2026 (3.0×10²⁰).
equation: C_max = the most capable single thinker: the biggest brain's signals a second, or after 2008 the largest supercomputer / AI cluster
cite: TOP500 Supercomputer Sites (2010–2024). Linpack Rmax historical #1 benchmarks (Tianhe-1A, Titan, Fugaku). | Epoch AI (2025).

basis: Total DNA in the biosphere, scaled by cell counts at two bits per base pair.
equation: H_DNA = N_prok × 6×10⁶ bits + N_euk × 1.9×10⁸ bits (2 bits per DNA letter)

basis: World capacity to store information outside bodies.
equation: M_outside = installed storage of each era (marks, tablets, books, disks); today 15 zettabytes

basis: Short-lived state per cell and per neuron, plus installed DRAM.
equation: M_active = 100 bits × N_prok + 1,000 × N_euk + 500 × N_neurons + computer memory (DRAM)

basis: Set by hand from the largest known group at each moment (colony, band, city, state, today's 8.1 billion people). No dedicated key source is recorded.
equation: N_group = largest group acting as one (set by hand)

basis: Mass-specific metabolic rates, primary production and maintenance power applied to biomass. Today: 14 TW microbes, 48.5 TW plant, fungal and other complex cells, 2.5 TW animals. Measured top down, plants and algae store about 130 TW as new growth (net primary production), twice this count; the gap is not yet reconciled.
equation: P_bio = P_microbes + P_other cells + P_animals

basis: Set by hand per era (fire, farming, coal, oil). Today's 19.5 TW matches the world's measured primary energy use; 1844 (0.85 TW) and 1890 (1.3 TW, interpolated) follow Our World in Data's world primary energy series (Smil): 0.83 TW in 1840, 0.89 TW in 1850, 1.5 TW around 1905. No source is recorded for other earlier moments.
equation: P_tech = primary energy people use (fire, fuel, electricity), set by hand per era
cite: Energy Institute (2024). Statistical Review of World Energy 2024: world primary energy use 620 EJ in 2023, about 19.6 TW.

basis: Today's 550 Gt carbon is the measured world total; earlier moments are set by hand, moment by moment.
equation: B = B_prok + B_wood + B_euk + B_animal

basis: A model assumption, now with sources for its shares. The 85% for microbes matches microbial genomes, which are about 85–90% genes (Koonin & Wolf 2008). The 15% for other cells sits between humans (about 8% under selection, Rands et al. 2014) and yeast, flies and worms (18–68%, Siepel et al. 2005). The share for algae and plant cells, most of the complex cells on Earth, is not measured.
equation: H_sel = 0.85 × microbial DNA bits + 0.15 × other DNA bits
cite: Koonin, E. V., & Wolf, Y. I. (2008). Genomics of bacteria and archaea. Nucleic Acids Research, 36(21), 6688–6719. | Rands, C. M., et al. (2014). 8.2% of the human genome is constrained. PLoS Genetics, 10(7), e1004525. | Siepel, A., et al. (2005). Evolutionarily conserved elements in vertebrate, insect, worm, and yeast genomes. Genome Research, 15(8), 1034–1050.

basis: Set by hand, now checked against gene catalogues. About 303 million distinct genes have already been sampled from the world's microbes (Coelho et al. 2022), about 6×10¹¹ bits. Today's 3.8×10¹² bits implies about 1.9 billion distinct genes, six times the sampled catalogue, which is plausible because sampling is far from complete. Earlier values are estimates.
equation: H_unique = distinct gene families × bits per family (set by hand)
cite: Coelho, L. P., et al. (2022). Towards the biogeography of prokaryotic genes. Nature, 601, 252–256. | Locey, K. J., & Lennon, J. T. (2016). Scaling laws predict global microbial diversity. PNAS, 113(21), 5970–5975.

basis: Long-term memory adds three stores: DNA, synapses (4.7 bits each, from spine sizes) and outside memory.
equation: M_kept = H_DNA + 4.7 bits × synapses + M_outside

basis: Animal power scales with animal biomass: 2 Gt carbon of animals today use 2.5 TW. The 2.5 TW is a model assumption.
equation: P_animals = (B_animal ÷ 2 Gt carbon) × 2.5 TW

basis: Total power is life's power plus technology's power.
equation: P = P_bio + P_tech

basis: Electricity used by computers and data centres; today 80 GW from data-centre electricity estimates.
equation: P_computers = electricity used by chips and data centres (set by hand per era)

basis: Electrical signals in plants, fungi, microbes and nerveless animals, set by hand. Trees alone give 3×10²⁰ to 3×10²¹ a second (Crowther et al. 2015). Potassium waves in bacterial biofilms could add 10²⁴ to 10²⁶ (Prindle et al. 2015), so today's 7×10²³ lies inside the range but depends on how much biofilm signalling is counted. Fungi and nerveless animals add little.
equation: C_electric = cells that signal electrically × signals per cell per second (set by hand)
cite: Prindle, A., et al. (2015). Ion channels enable electrical communication in bacterial communities. Nature, 527, 59–63.

basis: How far the most capable single thinker sits above a typical cell, in digits.
equation: R = log₁₀(C_max ÷ 1,000 signals a second)

basis: A model assumption: DNA survives as long as its lineage, 50 million years for modern lineages. Fossil surveys give about 11 million years for an average marine species and 28 million for a genus (mean; the median genus lasts 11 million) (Raup 1978), so 50 million is longer than an average genus. Conserved genes such as ribosomal RNA last billions of years, so the level chosen sets the answer.
equation: Φ = H_DNA × lineage lifetime in years
cite: Raup, D. M. (1978). Cohort analysis of generic survivorship. Paleobiology, 4(1), 1–15.

basis: Set by hand for each moment, anchored by the model's builder to these temperature reconstructions.
equation: T = global mean surface temperature (set by hand from reconstructions)
cite: Scotese, C. R., Song, H., Mills, B. J. W., & van der Meer, D. G. (2021). Phanerozoic paleotemperatures: the earth's changing climate during the last 540 million years. Earth-Science Reviews, 215, 103503. | Judd, E. J., et al. (2024). A 485-million-year history of Earth's surface temperature. Science, 385, eadk3705.

basis: Set by hand for each moment, anchored by the model's builder to these oxygen reconstructions.
equation: O₂ = share of oxygen in the air (set by hand from reconstructions)
cite: Lyons, T. W., Reinhard, C. T., & Planavsky, N. J. (2014). The rise of oxygen in Earth's early ocean and atmosphere. Nature, 506, 307–315. | Krause, A. J., Mills, B. J. W., Merdith, A. S., Lenton, T. M., & Poulton, S. W. (2022). Extreme variability in atmospheric oxygen levels in the late Precambrian. Science Advances, 8, eabm8191.

basis: Set by hand for each moment, anchored by the model's builder to this CO₂ compilation (about 1,500 estimates from 112 studies).
equation: CO₂ = carbon dioxide in the air, parts per million (set by hand from reconstructions)
cite: Foster, G. L., Royer, D. L., & Lunt, D. J. (2017). Future climate forcing potentially without precedent in the last 420 million years. Nature Communications, 8, 14845.
